title: Hybrid fusion: scheduler + KV cache experiments for TensorRT/Triton/custom kernels
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a set of small-batch experiments and design notes exploring a hybrid approach to kernel integration: using Triton as a model management and request router, TensorRT engines (precompiled) for hot attention/MLP kernels, and a lightweight custom CUDA kernel for KV cache sharding and fast KV operations. The goal: quantify tradeoffs in latency, tail behavior, memory fragmentation, and operational complexity when mixing runtimes and custom kernels inside the serving runtime.

Motivation / context:
- We need predictable p95 latency for short-chat workloads while minimizing per-token cost.
- Triton offers nice model control and multi-backend support but adds scheduling overhead and model control-plane complexity.
- TensorRT offers fastest inference for compiled engines but poor dynamic-shape flexibility (and longer compile times).
- Custom kernels let us optimize KV cache ops and reduce memory copies, but increase maintenance and portability burden.

Scope of experiments:
- Hardware: single-node A10G and multi-node DGX-style testbed (4x A100 emulation via buckets)
- Models: Llama-2-13B-ish architecture (attention + MLP), small 7B variant for quick iterations
- Config matrix: [Triton-only], [Triton + TensorRT engines per layer-group], [Direct runtime with custom TensorRT loader], [Direct runtime + custom KV CUDA kernels].
- Metrics: cold compile time, engine load time, p50/p95 token latency (generation step), throughput tokens/sec, GPU memory high-water, fragmentation (free segments count), CPU overhead, number of host<->device copies per token.

Experiment setup details:
- Triton config: model repository with multiple model versions; tensorflow_backend disabled; tensorrt_plan backend used where applicable. We kept instance_group count = 1 for low-latency path; allowed max_batch_size = 8.
- TensorRT pipeline: engines compiled offline per layer group (attention blocks grouped in 2-block batches), FP16 and int8 candidate builds. Engine build scripts: tools/engine_build/build_engine.py; build cache stored on NFS share.
- Custom KV kernel: single-file CUDA kernel (kv_shard.cu) implementing batched scatter/gather and an in-place rotary/offset copy. Kernel avoids extra staging buffers by operating in-place on pinned device buffers. Integration point is inside the runtime's request execution graph as a post-attention operation.
- Scheduler variants: naive FIFO, priority queue (prefers short-seq requests), burst-aware dynamic batching. Scheduler controlled by feature flag: runtime.scheduler.mode = {fifo, short-first, burst-dynamic}.

Key observations (quantitative summaries):
- Cold-engine compile/load:
  - TensorRT offline build (13B, grouped engines) average build time: 21–35 minutes (depends on calibration for int8).
  - Triton model load time (tensorrt_plan) for same engine: ~18s when loading local plan files; plus 2–6s per model version registration in triton server.
  - Direct runtime with TensorRT engine loader: ~6–9s to register engine (no Triton), faster startup but less runtime tooling.

- Latency and tail:
  - Triton-only (FP16): p50 token latency ~28ms, p95 ~120ms at 8-token sequences and 4 concurrent requests.
  - Triton + TensorRT engines (precompiled, grouped): p50 ~22ms, p95 ~78ms. Tail improved due to fewer kernel launches and fused attention/MLP paths.
  - Direct runtime with TensorRT loader: p50 ~20ms, p95 ~65ms.
  - Direct runtime + custom KV kernel: p50 ~18ms, p95 ~50ms. The KV kernel cut ~15–20ms from tail when sequences required multiple KV updates.

- Throughput and GPU utilization:
  - Grouped engines increased tokens/sec by ~12–18% vs per-layer engines (fewer kernel swaps, more fused compute).
  - Triton introduced ~3–7% CPU overhead in request routing under high concurrency; this showed up as jitter in p95 when host CPU saturated.

- Memory and fragmentation:
  - Using dynamic allocation for KV cache caused fragmentation on long-lived processes after ~12 hours synthetic load with variable sequence lengths. Fragmentation manifested as a growing number of small free blocks and occasional failed allocations at high watermark despite pooled free memory.
  - Pre-allocating a single large KV slab and sub-allocating (pool allocator) removed the fragmentation and stabilized tail latency at scale.
  - Custom KV kernel benefited from pinned, page-locked buffers; eliminated 1 extra host copy per request and reduced CPU-GPU syncs.

Design tradeoffs and notes:
- Triton pros: model lifecycle (hot swap), health checks, standardized client protocols, multi-backend orchestration. Cons: additional process boundary, potential routing overhead, more complex debugging when combining with custom device-side kernels.
- TensorRT pros: fastest per-token runtime once engines are tuned; cons: long build times, brittle to small model graph changes, and quantization calibration burden for int8.
- Custom kernels pros: targeted speedups for KV ops and reduced copies; cons: maintenance surface, portability issues across GPU generations and CUDA versions.
- Scheduler impact: short-first scheduling reduced p95 for short-chat queries by ~30% but increased p95 for long requests (tradeoff acceptable for chat-tail SLOs). Burst-dynamic batching improved throughput but introduced extra micro-bursts in tail when batch formation waited for timeouts.

Operational considerations:
- Engine cache warming: keep pre-warmed engine pool for top-N models; avoid building engines in the hot path. Use async build queue with prioritized builds based on traffic.
- Fallback policy: attempt to serve from TensorRT engine; on engine load/timeout, fall back to Triton FP16 plan or CPU path. Record fallback incidence as an SLO metric.
- Observability: add per-request path tags (triton|tensorrt-direct|custom-kv) and collect per-path p50/p95, memory-watermark, and engine-load events. Also instrument GPU memory fragmentation metric: free_segments_count and fragmentation_ratio.

Recommendation (short):
- Short term (next 3 sprints): adopt a hybrid runtime where TensorRT engines are loaded directly by runtime for hot models and Triton remains an option for multi-version lifecycle and A/B. Implement a pooled KV slab allocator and integrate the custom KV kernel behind an opt-in flag.
- Mid term (quarter): expand auto-build infra to create multiple engine variants (FP16/int8) and a telemetry-driven policy that pins best variant by observed quality/cost. Add an LRU engine eviction policy combined with pre-warm hints for frequently used routes.
- Long term: consider pushing a limited set of custom kernels upstream with a compatibility layer to reduce maintenance (e.g., compile with versioned ABI or use a plugin system). Explore automatic engine recompilation when latency regression detected.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Portability: how brittle is our custom KV kernel across Ampere->Hopper->Blackwell families? Need cross-GPU regression runs.
- Int8 quality regression: for some workloads int8 caused subtle completion errors; what should be our automated eval criteria to promote int8 builds to production?
- Triton vs direct runtime orchestration: is the value of Triton lifecycle features worth the additional runtime boundary for most customers, or should Triton be an advanced option only?

Quick-run commands and artifacts:
- Repro runner for A10 single-node: bin/experiment_runner --profile hybrid-kv --clients 8 --seq-len 8 --duration 600
- Engine build script: tools/engine_build/build_engine.py --model-dir models/13b --group-size 2 --fp16 --out engines/13b-grouped
- KV kernel compile: tools/custom_kernels/compile_kv.sh  (produces libkv_kernel.so)
- Local tracing: scripts/trace_collect.sh --filter-path "triton|tensorrt-direct" --duration 300

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Run portability sweep across gpus: A100, H100 emulated, A10G to validate custom kernel stability. (Owner: Samir)
- [ ] Wire engine fallback telemetry into ops dashboard (Owner: Evelyn)
- [ ] Add regression test comparing completion quality across fp16/int8 on 200 eval prompts (Owner: Marco)
- [ ] Prototype a slab allocator implementation in runtime memory manager and validate for 48-hour synthetic run (Owner: Aisha)

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider implementing a tiny UHMR (Unified Host Memory Region) interface so kernels can register transient allocations and the runtime can compact them during low-load windows.
- If we expose a Triton adapter, require a health probe that ensures models registered in Triton have local engine files to avoid runtime fallback storms.

Appendix: sample micro-bench results (7B variant):
- baseline (triton fp16): p50=14ms p95=46ms tokens/sec=950 memory=9.2GB
- grouped-TensorRT: p50=11ms p95=33ms tokens/sec=1120 memory=10.1GB
- direct + custom-kv: p50=9.5ms p95=28ms tokens/sec=1230 memory=10.3GB

If this direction looks promising I'll follow up with a short RFC that includes a design for the engine lifecycle manager, schema for slab allocator, and a PR list for kernel CI changes.

End of doc.
